notes: An album converts in minutes instead of an hour. Three things were slow and all three are fixed: a song’s audio is now pulled four ranges at a time instead of one after another, several songs convert at once instead of one waiting for the last, and the encoders run on their own threads instead of on the one thread every tap has to get through.

The encoders moved off the app’s thread. FLAC and MP3 are seconds of solid arithmetic per song — about two hours of it across a 32-song album — and running that where the interface lives is why a long run felt like the app had stopped. The work now runs in worker threads, by the same encoders: the files are the same files, byte for byte.

A run keeps going in the background. Start an album, leave the app, put the phone down: the run holds itself open (the same Web Lock the compressor uses), keeps its progress in the notification, and the songs are in your library when you come back.

On Android the app also keeps the device awake for the length of a run and hands it straight back when the last song lands — a locked screen no longer stops a download. (That part ships with the next app build; the release itself uses the lock the browser honours.)

The lane count follows the device: two songs at a time on a small phone, three on a normal one, four on a roomy one — a song’s decoded audio is ~74 MB, so this is a memory number, and memory is what a phone runs out of first.

Two songs of one album can no longer be handed the same upload. The claim on a source is taken before the download rather than after it, which is what a run of several songs at once needs to stay honest.
